Date: 2025-08-14
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Marques (Victor Labs - ML Ops), Samir Rao (Victor Labs - InfoSec), Priya Nair (Victor Labs - CTO), Carlos Vega (Victor Labs - Infra)
summary: Intro discovery for deploying Redwood in Victor Labs' closed facility (no internet egress). Main topics: deployment topology options (airgapped private control plane vs fully on-prem), update/patch cadence & signed firmware, KMS/HSM and key management, SOC2/ISO evidence, hardware compatibility and GPU constraints, fallback/failover and rolling updates. Action items captured and next steps to share docs and sizing.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and with me is Maya Chen, our systems SE.
[00:08] Maya Chen: Hi all. Thanks for taking the time.
[00:11] Dr. Elena Marques: Hi, thanks. We'll kick off. We're evaluating options for running models inside our secure site.
[00:18] Jordan Patel: Great. Can you give us a snapshot of the constraints — network, hardware, patch windows?
[00:26] Carlos Vega: Yeah. We're completely closed — no outbound internet. Only air-gapped USB or physical media to push updates. GPU estate is mixed: a couple of A100s, some T4s for legacy, and two L40s coming next quarter.
[00:39] Samir Rao: From infosec perspective we need signed images, HSM-backed keys, and auditable install steps. SOC2 evidence is required — and we have a pretty strict change control window: monthly maintenance window, emergency-only patches require a 4-person approval chain.
[00:56] Maya Chen: Understood. We support private deployments where the control plane can either be fully customer-hosted or a private control plane with no egress; both ways we can accommodate signed bundles for offline install.
[01:08] Priya Nair: When you say "signed bundles", what does the workflow look like? We can't accept a direct push from a hosted Redwood control plane.
[01:16] Maya Chen: Right — we create a release artifact, signed by Redwood's release key. Your ops team pulls it onto a USB or SCCM-like airgap process, verifies signature against your HSM, and installs. We can also integrate with your HSM to verify at install time if you prefer.
[01:29] Dr. Elena Marques: So the verification step would run locally against our HSM — no shared secrets are required?
[01:34] Maya Chen: Correct. The signatures are public-key based; you only need to provision the verification key in the HSM or in your key store. We don't need your private keys.
[01:43] Jordan Patel: To help us size and recommend a deployment pattern — could you describe expected throughput and latency SLAs?
[01:50] Dr. Elena Marques: For our initial use case — document triage and embedding search — we expect around 10–20 concurrent users with bursts up to 60 qps for embeddings during indexing windows. Latency target is sub-200ms 95th for simple generation and <100ms for embedding calls, if possible.
[02:09] Maya Chen: Got it. That profile points to keeping at least one A100 for generation and maybe a couple of L40s for embedding throughput, depending on quantization. We can recommend fp16 or 4-bit quant profiles to improve throughput; we'll put numbers into a sizing spreadsheet.
[02:24] Samir Rao: How do you handle KV cache and state? We need to ensure there's no data leaving the site.
[02:30] Maya Chen: All KV cache and ephemeral state stays on the host; no telemetry or token-level logs are shipped out unless you opt in. For private deployments we ship an ops agent that's disabled by default; you can enable local telemetry to a local Elasticsearch or our console if you give us read-only log export files.
[02:47] Carlos Vega: What about model updates — if we find a bug or need a patch, how fast can we get a new model into our facility?
[02:53] Jordan Patel: That depends on your change control. We can prepare an emergency signed patch and ship via encrypted USB, but our internal release cadence is bi-weekly; emergency hotfixes are available and will pass the same signing process. Typical lead time for non-emergency versions is 2–3 weeks.
[03:08] Priya Nair: Do you support custom models hosted purely locally? We may want to run our own fine-tuned variants.
[03:14] Maya Chen: Yes. You can bring-your-own-model. The runtime supports loading customer model artifacts. We can provide conversion scripts for optimized kernels and quantization guidance. If you want Redwood to manage model versioning locally, we can provide the same rollout API but with local control plane endpoints.
[03:29] Dr. Elena Marques: What about licensing and telemetry — redwood will not pull usage data out of our site?
[03:34] Jordan Patel: Only what you allow. For hosted customers we do token-level billing telemetry; in private offline deployments we can either run a local billing collector that you export periodically, or we can operate on committed capacity contracts with periodic offline usage reporting. Nothing is sent automatically.
[03:49] Samir Rao: On the compliance side we need to see: signed audit logs, SSO/SAML integration for user provisioning, RBAC for engineers, and encryption at rest using our keys. Can you support KMS/HSM integrations?
[04:01] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We have connectors for common on-prem HSMs and for cloud KMS when available. For offline installs we can accept a key-wrap workflow where you wrap a data key with your HSM and keep the unwrapped key local. RBAC and SAML are configurable — we can authenticate against your IdP; for fully air-gapped you can run a local IdP or we can federate via SAML metadata exchange during the initial setup.
[04:22] Priya Nair: What about the console — is it completely blocked for our site?
[04:26] Maya Chen: The Redwood Console is available as a UI you can host behind your network. We can deploy a console instance that talks only to the local control plane. Alternatively, we can provide exported dashboards in static form if you prefer no UI.
[04:39] Carlos Vega: Firmware and driver updates are managed by our firmware team; we can't accept arbitrary kernel modules. How does Redwood's runtime interact with NVIDIA drivers or kernel requirements?
[04:48] Maya Chen: Our runtime has kernel and driver dependencies documented in the install guide. We don't require custom kernel modules; we rely on NVIDIA's standard drivers and CUDA stacks. For older drivers we have compatibility layers, but certain optimizations (like fused kernels) need newer drivers. We'll include a compatibility matrix in the sizing doc.
[05:05] Dr. Elena Marques: How do you handle rollbacks? If an update causes inference regressions, can we pin to an earlier model?
[05:11] Jordan Patel: Yes — on private deployments you can pin model versions locally. Our rollout tooling supports canary or immediate rollbacks and you can run pre-deploy sanity checks.
[05:20] Samir Rao: Network segmentation — we enforce that management plane and inference plane are separated. Does Redwood require management access to inference nodes?
[05:27] Maya Chen: No; for air-gapped we recommend management plane be within the same network segment but logically separate. We don't need remote access — installs can be performed by your team using our signed artifacts. If you want Redwood support, we can provide a jumpbox model where support engineers are given temporary console access via a pre-shared ephemeral key and require explicit approvals.
[05:47] Priya Nair: Can we run a small pilot with one generation model and one embedding model inside our cluster with a CAC card authentication for the ops users?
[05:56] Jordan Patel: Yes, pilot works. We'll scope a two-week PoC: sizing, deployment, and performance run. Maya will provide the technical checklist.
[06:02] Maya Chen: I'll also include recommended quant profiles per GPU variant and expected token/sec numbers.
[06:07] Dr. Elena Marques: One concern — model provenance. We need to ensure models haven't been altered in transit and we can verify their checksum.
[06:13] Maya Chen: Checksums are included and signatures. You can verify SHA sums locally.
[06:17] Carlos Vega: Are there any known blockers for older firmware on A100s? We have a couple in rack with an older microcode.
[06:24] Maya Chen: Older firmware may affect certain kernels; we'll flag that in the compatibility matrix. If you can't update firmware quickly, we can recommend fallback execution paths that avoid the optimized kernels at some cost to throughput.
[06:38] Samir Rao: About legal — we will need indemnities and understanding around data residency. Can you supply standard Enterprise contract with CL clauses for regulated PII handling?
[06:48] Jordan Patel: Yes — our enterprise legal team has a template for private deployments covering data residency and liability. We'll include it in the packet Jordan sends.
[06:56] Dr. Elena Marques: Quick question on monitoring — we want traces and per-request latency but stored only on-prem. Does Redwood support a local prometheus + jaeger stack?
[07:05] Maya Chen: We can push metrics to local Prometheus and traces to Jaeger/Zipkin hosted in your environment; our agents export via HTTP to your collector.
[07:13] Priya Nair: If we later want to move to a dedicated Redwood-hosted model, is there an easy migration path?
[07:18] Jordan Patel: Yes — the API and configs are the same across hosted/dedicated/private. The deployment abstraction makes migration straightforward — you can pin versions, switch routing policies, and Redwood can assist with lift-and-shift.
[07:29] Dr. Elena Marques: On the sizing note, can you give a back-of-the-envelope cost for a reserved capacity equivalent in our site?
[07:36] Jordan Patel: For an on-prem contract we usually price by reserved capacity and support tier. I'll send a ballpark pricing for 1 A100-equivalent reserved capacity plus support. It will be indicative until we get exact telemetry.
[07:47] Carlos Vega: For updates that require a reboot, our maintenance window is Sunday 02:00-06:00 local. How do you handle stateful hot restarts for models with hot KV cache?
[07:57] Maya Chen: We support a warm restart where KV cache is checkpointed locally and restored. For critical services we recommend a small cluster to allow rolling restarts during your window. We'll document the restore steps.
[08:10] Samir Rao: A gotcha — our compliance team will want to see cryptographic attestations that the binaries match Redwood's release. Do you provide signed attestations that tie to a reproducible build hash?
[08:20] Maya Chen: Yes — we can supply SBOMs, reproducible build hashes, and signed attestations for each release.
[08:28] Dr. Elena Marques: We're worried about model regression when quantizing. Do you run regression tests or provide eval harnesses?
[08:34] Maya Chen: Our Optimize team generates quantization-aware evals and can run callbacks on your prompt set. For pilots, we can run a small battery of prompts and share comparative outputs so you can validate quality before rollout.
[08:47] Jordan Patel: Let's recap next steps quickly. We'll send a compliance packet (SOC2, SBOM, signatures), Maya will send sizing and compatibility matrix, and Victor Labs will share HW inventory and change window policy.
[08:58] Dr. Elena Marques: That sounds good. Also, can you include an example signed USB workflow so our ops can trial the install steps?
[09:05] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include an install runbook with the exact commands and verification steps.
[09:10] Priya Nair: One more — what's the best phone/email if we hit a blocker during install?
[09:14] Jordan Patel: I'll include a 24/7 escalation contact for the pilot and account team support lines in the packet.
[09:20] Carlos Vega: If we do a PoC, are there any NDA or export constraints we should sign first? We operate with certain export restrictions on model weights.
[09:29] Jordan Patel: We can process an NDA. For export restricted weights we can agree to run only within your facility and accept necessary contractual clauses.
[09:36] Samir Rao: A tiny nit — does Redwood runtime collect any randomness or telemetry that could leak?
[09:40] Maya Chen: No randomness is exfiltrated. Telemetry is opt-in; local-only. We'll provide the telemetry schema so you can review fields.
[09:50] Dr. Elena Marques: Great. Let's set the PoC dates after we review the docs. How long do you need to prepare the signed bundles?
[09:56] Maya Chen: For pilot artifacts probably 3–5 business days after we have HW inventory and chosen models. For a fully integrated signed release it's usually 7–10 business days.
[10:09] Jordan Patel: OK — we'll follow up with the packet and proposed PoC week. Thanks everyone.
[10:13] Dr. Elena Marques: Thanks, much appreciated.
[10:15] Priya Nair: Thanks.
[10:18] Samir Rao: Bye.
[10:20] Jordan Patel: Bye all.
